{{For|the political ideology that favours Quebec remaining within the Canadian federation rather than pursuing independence|Federalism in Quebec}}

{{Politics of Canada}}
{{Constitutional history of Canada}}

'''Federalism in Canada''' ({{Langx|fr|Le fédéralisme au Canada}}) involves the current nature and historical development of the federal system in Canada.

Canada is a federation with eleven components:  the national [[Government of Canada]] and ten [[Provinces and territories of Canada|provincial governments]]. All eleven governments derive their authority from the [[Constitution of Canada]]. There are also three territorial governments in the far north, which exercise powers delegated by the [[Parliament of Canada|federal parliament]], and municipal governments which exercise powers delegated by the province or territory. Each jurisdiction is generally independent from the others in its realm of legislative authority.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sUwOAAAAQAAJ|title=And no one cheered: federalism, democracy, and the Constitution Act|last=Banting|first=Keith G.|author2=Simeon, Richard|publisher=Methuen|year=1983|isbn=0-458-95950-2|location=Toronto|pages=14, 16}}</ref> The division of powers between the federal government and the provincial governments is based on the principle of exhaustive distribution:  all legal issues are assigned to either the federal Parliament or the provincial Legislatures.

The division of powers is set out in the ''[[Constitution Act, 1867]]'' (originally called the ''British North America Act, 1867''), a key document in the Constitution of Canada.  Some amendments to the division of powers have been made in the past century and a half, but the 1867 act still sets out the basic framework of the federal and provincial legislative jurisdictions. The division of power is reliant upon the "division" of the unitary [[Monarchy of Canada|Canadian Crown]] and, with it, of [[Canadian sovereignty]], among the country's 11 jurisdictions.

The [[Federation|federal]] nature of the Canadian constitution was a response to the [[Colonialism|colonial]]-era diversity of [[the Maritimes]] and the [[Province of Canada]], particularly the sharp distinction between the French-speaking inhabitants of [[Lower Canada]] and the English-speaking inhabitants of [[Upper Canada]] and the Maritimes. [[John A. Macdonald]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/macdonald_john_alexander_12E.html|title=Biography – MACDONALD, Sir JOHN ALEXANDER – Volume XII (1891-1900) – Dictionary of Canadian Biography|website=biographi.ca|access-date=1 February 2019}}</ref> Canada's first [[Prime Minister of Canada|prime minister]], originally favoured a [[Unitary state|unitary]] system.<ref>{{Cite web| title=John A. Macdonald on the Federal System| url=http://www.macdonald-laurier.ca/en/macdonald/macdonald-speeches-1823| publisher=The Historica-Dominion Institute| access-date=24 December 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130627210817/http://www.macdonald-laurier.ca/en/macdonald/macdonald-speeches-1823| archive-date=27 June 2013| url-status=dead}}, quoting {{cite book| url=https://archive.org/details/parliamentaryde09parlgoog| title=Parliamentary Debates on the Subject of the Confederation of the British North American Provinces—3rd Session, 8th Provincial Parliament of Canada| year=1865| publisher=Hunter, Rose & Co.| pages=[https://archive.org/details/parliamentaryde09parlgoog/page/n44 29]–45| location=Quebec}}</ref>

== History ==
{{Further|Constitutional history of Canada}}

=== Origins ===
{{see also|Canadian Confederation|Post-Confederation Canada (1867–1914)}}

[[File:John A Macdonald (ca. 1875).jpg|thumb|alt=Formal photograph of John A. Macdonald|Sir [[John A. Macdonald]]]]

The foundations of Canadian federalism were laid at the [[Quebec Conference, 1864|Quebec Conference of 1864]]. The [[Quebec Resolutions]] were a compromise between those who wanted sovereignty vested in the federal government and those who wanted it vested in the provinces. The compromise based the federation on the constitution of the [[British Empire]], under which the legal sovereignty of imperial power was modified by the conventions of colonial [[responsible government]], making colonies of settlement (such as those of [[British North America]]) self-governing in domestic affairs. A lengthy political process ensued before the [[Quebec Resolutions]] became the ''[[British North America Act 1867]]''. This process was dominated by [[John A. Macdonald]], who joined British officials in attempting to make the federation more centralized than that envisaged by the Resolutions.{{sfn|Romney|1999|pp=[https://archive.org/details/gettingitwrongho0000romn/page/100 100]–102}}

The resulting constitution was couched in more centralist terms than intended. As prime minister, Macdonald tried to exploit this discrepancy to impose his centralist ideal against chief opponent [[Oliver Mowat]]. In a series of political battles and court cases from 1872 to 1896,{{efn|The federal regulation of [[Trade and commerce (Canadian law)|trade and commerce]] was circumscribed by the provincial [[property and civil rights]] power as a result of ''[[Citizen's Insurance Co. v. Parsons]]'',<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Citizens Insurance Company of Canada and The Queen Insurance Company v Parsons| link=Citizen's Insurance Co. v. Parsons| court=UKPC| year=1881| num=49| parallelcite=(1881) 7 A.C. 96| date=26 November 1881| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada| format=1}}</ref> disallowance and reservation of provincial statutes was curtailed as a political consequence of ''[[McLaren v. Caldwell]]'',<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=Caldwell and another v McLaren| link=McLaren v. Caldwell| court=UKPC| year=1884| num=21| parallelcite=(1884) 9 A.C. 392| date=7 April 1884| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada| format=1}}</ref>{{sfn|Lamot|1998|p=125}} and the [[double aspect]] doctrine was introduced into Canadian jurisprudence via ''[[Hodge v. The Queen]]''.<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=Hodge v The Queen (Canada)| link=Hodge v. The Queen| court=UKPC| year=1883| num=59| date=15 December 1883|pinpoint= pp. 9–10| parallelcite=9 App Cas 117| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Ontario| format=1}}</ref> Not all rulings, however, went in the provinces' favour. ''[[Russell v. The Queen]]'' established the right of the federal parliament to make laws applicable in the provinces if those laws relate to a concern that exists in all jurisdictions of the country<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=Charles Russell v The Queen (New Brunswick)| link=Russell v. The Queen| court=UKPC| year=1882| num=33| parallelcite=[1882] 7 App Cas 829, 8 CRAC 502|pinpoint= pp. 17–18| date=23 June 1882| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada| format=1}}</ref> and in ''[[Royal Bank of Canada v. The King]]'' the provinces were held not to possess the power to affect extraprovincial contract rights.<ref name=RBC-King group=nb/> [[Pith and substance]], used to determine under which crown a given piece of legislation falls, was introduced in ''[[Cushing v. Dupuy]]''.<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=Cushing v Dupuy| link= Cushing v. Dupuy|court=UKPC| year=1880| num=22| date=15 April 1880| parallelcite=(1880) 5 AC 409|pinpoint= pp. 3{{endash}}4| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|juris=Quebec| format=1}}</ref>}} Mowat reversed Macdonald's early victories and entrenched the co-ordinated sovereignty which he saw in the Quebec Resolutions.<ref>{{Cite book| last=Romney| first=Paul| title=Mr Attorney: The Attorney-General for Ontario in court, cabinet and legislature, 1791-1899| publisher=University of Toronto Press| year=1986| location=Toronto| page=240{{endash}}281}}</ref> In 1888, [[Edward Blake]] summarized that view: "[It is] a federal as distinguished from a legislative union, but a union composed of several existing and continuing entities ... [The provinces are] not fractions of a unit but units of a multiple. The Dominion is the multiple and each province is a unit of that multiple ..."<ref>{{cite book| author=Edward Blake| author-link=Edward Blake| title=The St. Catharine's Milling and Lumber Company v. the Queen: Argument of Mr. Blake, of counsel for Ontario| url=https://archive.org/stream/cihm_00164#page/6/mode/2up|page=6| publisher=Press of the Budget| year=1888| location=Toronto| isbn=9780665001642}}</ref> The accession of [[Wilfrid Laurier]] as prime minister inaugurated a new phase of constitutional consensus, marked by a more-egalitarian relationship between the jurisdictions. The federal government's quasi-imperial powers of [[Disallowance and reservation in Canada|disallowance and reservation]], which Macdonald used in his efforts to impose a centralised government, fell into disuse.

=== 1914–1960 ===
{{see also|Canada in the World Wars and Interwar Years|History of Canada (1945–1960)}}

During [[World War I]], the federal Crown's power was extended with the introduction of [[income tax]]es and passage of the ''[[War Measures Act]]'', the scope of which was determined by several court cases.{{efn|The ''[[Board of Commerce case]]'' affirmed that only a national emergency warranted the curtailment of citizens' rights by the federal parliament,<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Attorney General of Canada v The Attorney General of Alberta and others ("Board of Commerce case")| link=Canada v. Alberta| court=UKPC| year=1921| num=107| date=8 November 1921| parallelcite=[1922] 1 A.C. 191|pinpoint=p. 4| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada| format=1}}</ref> subsequently reaffirmed by ''[[Fort Frances Pulp and Paper v. Manitoba Free Press]]'',<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Fort Frances Pulp and Paper Company Limited v The Manitoba Free Press Company Limited and others| link=Fort Frances Pulp and Paper v. Manitoba Free Press| court=UKPC| year=1923| num=64| date=25 July 1923| parallelcite=[1923] A.C. 695|pinpoint = p. 6| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Ontario| format=1}}</ref> and was held to even include amending Acts of Parliament through regulations.<ref group=nb>{{cite CanLII|litigants=In Re George Edwin Gray|link=|year=1918|court=scc|num=86|format=canlii|pinpoint=pp. 167{{endash}}173, 180{{endash}}183|parallelcite=57 SCR 150|date=19 July 1918 }}, drawing on {{cite BAILII|litigants=R v Halliday|link=|court=UKHL|year=1917|num=1|parallelcite= [1917] AC 260 |date=1 May 1917}}</ref> However, ''[[Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider]]'',<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Toronto Electric Commissioners v Colin G. Snider and others| link=Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider| court=UKPC| year=1925| num=2| parallelcite=[1925] AC 396| date=20 January 1925| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Ontario| format=1}}</ref> held that such emergencies could not be used to unreasonably intrude on the provinces' [[property and civil rights]] power.}} The constitution's restrictions of parliamentary power were affirmed in 1919 when, in the ''Initiatives and Referendums Reference'', a Manitoba act providing for [[Direct democracy|direct legislation]] by way of [[Popular initiative|initiative]]s and [[referendum]]s was ruled unconstitutional by the Privy Council on the grounds that a provincial viceroy (even one advised by responsible ministers) could not permit "the abrogation of any power which the Crown possesses through a person directly representing it".<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=In the matter of The Initiative and Referendum Act being Chapter 59 of the Acts of Legislative Assembly of Manitoba 6 George V.| court=UKPC| year=1919| num=60| date=3 July 1919| parallelcite=[1919] AC 935| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Manitoba| format=1}}</ref> Social and technological changes also worked their way into constitutional authority; the ''[[Radio Reference]]'' found that federal jurisdiction extended to [[broadcasting]],<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Attorney General of Quebec v The Attorney General of Canada and others ("Radio Reference")| link= Radio Reference|court=UKPC| year=1932| num=7| date=9 February 1932| parallelcite=[1932] A.C. 304| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada| format=1}}</ref> and the ''[[In re Regulation and Control of Aeronautics in Canada|Aeronautics Reference]]'' found the same for [[aeronautics]].<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Attorney-General Canada v The Attorney-General of Ontario and others ("Aeronautics Reference")| link=In re Regulation and Control of Aeronautics in Canada| court=UKPC| year=1931| num=93| date=22 October 1931| parallelcite=[1932] A.C. 54| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada| format=1}}</ref>

[[File:Dominion-Provincial Conference.JPG|thumb|left|alt=Large group photograph|Dominion-Provincial Conference, 1927]]

In 1926, the [[King–Byng Affair]] resulted in a [[constitutional crisis]] which was the impetus for changes in the relationship between the [[Governor General of Canada|governor general]] and the [[Prime Minister of Canada|prime minister]]. Although its key aspects were political in nature, its constitutional aspects continue to be debated.<ref>{{Citation| last=Forsey| first=Eugene| author-link=Eugene Forsey| date=1 October 2010| editor-last=Forsey| editor-first=Helen|  title=As David Johnson Enters Rideau Hall...| periodical=The Monitor| location=Ottawa| publisher=Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives| url=http://www.policyalternatives.ca/publications/monitor/david-johnson-enters-rideau-hall| access-date=8 August 2012}}</ref> One result was the [[Balfour Declaration of 1926|Balfour Declaration]] issued later that year, whose principles were eventually codified in the [[Statute of Westminster 1931]]. It, and the repeal of the ''[[Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865]]'', gave the federal parliament the ability to make extraterritorial laws and abolish appeals to the [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council]]. Criminal appeals were abolished in 1933,<ref group=na>Criminal Code Amendment Act, S.C. 1932–33, c. 53, s. 17</ref> but civil appeals continued until 1949.<ref group=na>Supreme Court Amendment Act, S.C. 1949 (2nd. session), c. 37, s. 3</ref> The last Privy Council ruling of constitutional significance occurred in 1954, in ''[[Winner v. S.M.T. (Eastern) Limited]]''.<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=Israel Winner (doing business under the name and style of Mackenzie Coach Lines) and others v. S.M.T. (Eastern) Limited and others| link= Winner v. S.M.T. (Eastern) Limited| court=UKPC| year=1954| num=8| date=22 February 1954| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada| format=1}}</ref> After that, the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] became the final court of appeal.

In 1937, [[Lieutenant Governor of Alberta]] [[John C. Bowen]] refused to give [[Royal Assent]] to three [[Legislative Assembly of Alberta]] bills. Two would have put the province's banks under the control of the provincial government; the third, the ''[[Accurate News and Information Act]]'', would have forced newspapers to print government rebuttals to stories the provincial [[Cabinet (government)|cabinet]] considered "inaccurate". All three bills were later declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court of Canada in ''[[Reference re Alberta Statutes]]'', which was upheld by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=Attorney General of Alberta v Attorney General of Canada| link=Reference re Alberta Statutes| court=UKPC| year=1938| num=46| date=14 July 1938| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada| format=1}}</ref>

[[World War II]]'s broader scope required passage of the ''[[National Resources Mobilization Act]]'' to supplement the powers in the ''War Measures Act'' to pursue the national war effort. The extent to which wartime federal power could expand was further clarified in the ''Chemicals Reference'' (which held that [[Order in Council|Orders in Council]] under the ''War Measures Act'' were equivalent to acts of parliament)<ref group=nb>{{cite CanLII| litigants=Reference as to the Validity of the Regulations in Relation to Chemicals Enacted by Order in Council and of an Order of the Controller of Chemicals Made Pursuant Thereto (The "Chemicals Reference")| year=1943| court=scc| num=1| format=canlii| parallelcite=[1943] SCR 1 |date=1 May 1943| courtname=auto}}</ref> and the ''Wartime Leasehold Regulations Reference'', which held that wartime regulations could displace provincial jurisdiction for the duration of an emergency.<ref group=nb>{{cite CanLII| litigants=Reference re Wartime Leasehold Regulations| year=1950| court=scc| num=27| format=canlii| parallelcite=[1950] SCR 124| date=1 March 1950| courtname=auto}}</ref> Additional measures were required in order to secure control of the economy during that time. Jurisdiction over unemployment insurance was transferred permanently to the federal sphere;<ref group=na>[[British North America Act 1940]] ([[3 & 4 Geo. 6]]. c. 36 (U.K.))</ref> the provinces surrendered their power to levy succession duties and personal and corporate income taxes for the duration of the war (and for one year afterwards) under the Wartime Tax Rental Agreement;<ref>{{Cite web| first=Claude| last=Bélanger| title=Canadian federalism, the Tax Rental Agreements of the period of 1941–1962 and fiscal federalism from 1962 to 1977| url=http://faculty.marianopolis.edu/c.belanger/quebechistory/federal/taxrent.htm| access-date=20 January 2012}}</ref> and labour relations were centralized under federal control with the [[Wartime Labour Relations Regulations]] (lasting until 1948), in which the provinces ceded their jurisdiction over all labour issues.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Ontario Labour Relations Board: History| url=http://www.olrb.gov.on.ca/english/AboutUs.htm| access-date=20 January 2012}}</ref>

Canada emerged from the war with better cooperation between the federal and provincial governments. This led to a [[welfare state]], a government-funded [[health care]] system and the adoption of [[Keynesian economics]]. In 1951 section 94A was added to the ''British North America Act, 1867'' to allow the Canadian parliament to provide for pensions.<ref group=na>[[British North America Act 1951]] ([[14 & 15 Geo. 6]]. c. 32 (U.K.))</ref> This was extended in 1964 to allow supplementary benefits, including disability and survivors' benefits.<ref group=na>[[British North America Act 1964]] (c. 73 (U.K.))</ref> The era saw an increase in [[First Ministers' Conference]]s to resolve federal-provincial issues. The [[Supreme Court of Canada]] became the court of final appeal after the 1949 abolition of appeals to the [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council]] and the federal parliament received the power to amend the constitution, limited to non-provincial matters and subject to other constraints.<ref group=na>[[British North America (No. 2) Act 1949]] ([[12, 13 & 14 Geo. 6]] c. 81 (U.K.))</ref>

=== 1960–1982 ===
{{see also|History of Canada (1960–1981)}}

1961 saw the last instance of a lieutenant governor reserving a bill passed by a provincial legislature. [[Frank Lindsay Bastedo]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Saskatchewan]], withheld Royal Assent and reserved Bill 5, ''An Act to Provide for the Alteration of Certain Mineral Contracts'', to the [[Governor-in-Council]] for review. According to Bastedo, "[T]his is a very important bill affecting hundreds of mineral contracts. It raises implications which throw grave doubts of the legislation being in the public interest. There is grave doubt as to its validity". The act was upheld in an Order in Council by the federal government.<ref>{{cite journal| last=Mallory | first= J. R.| author-link=James Mallory (jurist)| year=1961| title=The Lieutenant-Governor's Discretionary Powers: The Reservation of Bill 56| journal=Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science| volume=27| issue=4| pages=518–522| doi= 10.2307/139438| jstor=139438}}</ref><ref group=na>{{Citation| title=Order in Council P.C. 1961-675| url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/databases/canada-gazette/093/001060-119.01-e.php?image_id_nbr=763237&document_id_nbr=12435&f=g&PHPSESSID=keql83buk4g664q8setrf9jq87| date=13 May 1961| journal=Canada Gazette| access-date=19 August 2012}}</ref>

Parliament passed the ''[[Canadian Bill of Rights]]'', the first codification of rights by the federal government. Prime Minister [[Lester Pearson]] obtained passage of major social programs, including [[Medicare (Canada)|universal health care]] (a federal-provincial cost-sharing program), the [[Canada Pension Plan]] and [[Canada Student Loans]]. Quebec's [[Quiet Revolution]] encouraged increased administrative decentralization in Canada, with [[Quebec]] often opting out of federal initiatives and instituting its own (such as the [[Quebec Pension Plan]]). The [[Quebec sovereignty movement]] led to the victory of the [[Parti Québécois]] in the [[1976 Quebec general election|1976 Quebec election]], prompting consideration of further loosening ties with the rest of Canada; this was rejected in a [[1980 Quebec referendum|1980 referendum]].

During the premiership of [[Pierre Trudeau]], the federal government became more centralist. Canada experienced "conflictual federalism" from 1970 to 1984, generating tensions with Quebec and other provinces. The [[National Energy Program]] and other [[petroleum]] disputes sparked bitterness in [[Alberta]], [[Saskatchewan]] and [[Newfoundland and Labrador|Newfoundland]] toward the federal government.<ref>{{harvnb|Dyck|2012|pp=416–420}}</ref>

=== Patriation ===
{{main|Patriation}}

Although Canada achieved full status as a sovereign nation in the Statute of Westminster 1931, there was no consensus on a process to amend the constitution; attempts such as the 1965 [[Fulton–Favreau formula]] and the 1971 [[Victoria Charter]] failed to receive unanimous approval from both levels of government. When negotiations with the provinces again stalled in 1980, Trudeau threatened to take the case for patriation to the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|British parliament]] "[without] bothering to ask one premier". According to the federal cabinet and Crown counsel, if the British Crown (in council, in parliament, and on the bench) exercised sovereignty over Canada, it would do so only at the request of the federal ministers.<ref name=Romney273-4>{{Harvnb| Romney| 1999| pp=273–274}}</ref>

[[File:Chretientrudeau.jpg|thumb|left|alt=Pierre Trudeau and Jean Chrétien conferring, photographed from behind|[[Pierre Trudeau]] (left) and [[Jean Chrétien]] (right) at a session of the 1981 constitutional talks]]

Manitoba, Newfoundland and Quebec posed [[reference question]]s to their respective courts of appeal, in which five other provinces intervened in support. In his ruling, Justice Joseph O'Sullivan of the [[Manitoba Court of Appeal]] held that the federal government's position was incorrect; the constitutionally-entrenched principle of responsible government meant that "Canada had not one responsible government but eleven."<ref name=Romney273-4 /> Officials in the United Kingdom indicated that the British parliament was under no obligation to fulfill a request for legal changes desired by Trudeau, particularly if Canadian convention was not followed.<ref>{{cite web| first=Andrew| last=Heard| title=Canadian Independence| year=1990| location=Vancouver| publisher=Simon Fraser University| url=https://www.sfu.ca/~aheard/324/Independence.html| access-date=25 August 2010}}</ref> All rulings were appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada. In a decision later known as the ''[[Patriation Reference]]'', the court ruled that such a convention existed but did not prevent the federal parliament from attempting to amend the constitution without provincial consent and it was not the role of the courts to enforce constitutional conventions.

The Canadian parliament asked the British parliament to approve the ''[[Constitution Act, 1982]]'', which it did in passage of the ''[[Canada Act 1982]]''. This resulted in the introduction of the ''[[Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms]]'', the transfer of constitutional amendment to a Canadian framework and the addition of section 92A to the ''Constitution Act, 1867'', giving the provinces more jurisdiction over their natural resources.

=== After 1982 ===
{{see also|History of Canada (1982–1992)|History of Canada (1992–present)}}

The [[Progressive Conservative Party of Canada|Progressive Conservative Party]] under [[Joe Clark]] and [[Brian Mulroney]] favoured the devolution of power to the provinces, culminating in the failed [[Meech Lake Accord|Meech Lake]] and [[Charlottetown Accord|Charlottetown]] accords. After merging in 2003 with the heavily devolutionist [[Canadian Alliance]], the [[Conservative Party of Canada|Conservative Party]] under [[Stephen Harper]] has maintained the same stance. When Harper was appointed prime minister in 2006, the frequency of First Ministers' conferences declined significantly; inter-provincial cooperation increased with meetings of the [[Council of the Federation]], established by the provincial premiers, in 2003.

After the [[1995 Quebec referendum]] on sovereignty, Prime Minister [[Jean Chrétien]] limited the ability of the federal government to spend money in areas under provincial jurisdiction. In 1999 the federal government and all provincial governments except Quebec's agreed to the [[Social Union Framework Agreement]], which promoted common standards for social programmes across Canada.<ref>{{Cite journal| url=http://www.irpp.org/po/archive/nov98/noel.pdf| first=Alain| last=Noël| title=The Three Social Unions| journal=Policy Options| publisher=Institute for Research on Public Policy| volume=19| issue=9| date=November 1998| pages=26–29| language=fr| access-date=22 August 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071021050835/http://www.irpp.org/po/archive/nov98/noel.pdf| archive-date=21 October 2007| url-status=dead}}</ref> Former Prime Minister [[Paul Martin]] used the phrase "[[asymmetrical federalism]]" to describe this arrangement.<ref>{{Cite web| url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/Flexible+federalism.-a0141293686| title=Flexible federalism| via=The Free Library| access-date=19 January 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| url=http://www.optimumonline.ca/article.phtml?e=mesokurj&id=223&page=1| title=Who's afraid of Asymmetrical Federalism?| author=Douglas Brown| journal=Optimum Online| volume=35| issue=2| date=July 2005| page=2 et seq| access-date=19 January 2012}}</ref> The Supreme Court upholds the concepts of flexible federalism (where jurisdictions overlap) and cooperative federalism (where they can favourably interact),<ref>{{Cite web| url=http://www.thecourt.ca/2012/01/13/cooperative-federalism-the-securities-act-reference-2011-scc-66-a-rocky-road/| last=Hunter| first=Christopher| title=Cooperative Federalism & The Securities Act Reference: A Rocky Road| work=The Court| access-date=19 January 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120325150356/http://www.thecourt.ca/2012/01/13/cooperative-federalism-the-securities-act-reference-2011-scc-66-a-rocky-road/| archive-date=25 March 2012| url-status=dead}}</ref> as noted in ''[[Reference re Securities Act]]''.

== The Crown ==
{{Main|Monarchy of Canada|Monarchy in the Canadian provinces}}

As a [[federal monarchy]], the Canadian [[The Crown|Crown]] is present in all jurisdictions in the country,<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Attorney-General of Canada v. Higbie|link=|year=1944|source=scc|num=29|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1945] SCR 385|date=23 March 1944|courtname=auto|juris=}}</ref> with the [[Head of state|headship of state]] a part of all equally.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Roberts |first=Edward |author-link=Edward Roberts (Canadian politician) |title=Ensuring Constitutional Wisdom During Unconventional Times |journal=Canadian Parliamentary Review |page=13 |volume=23 |issue=1 |publisher=Commonwealth Parliamentary Association |location=Ottawa |year=2009 |url=http://www2.parl.gc.ca/Sites/LOP/Infoparl/32/1/32n1_09e_Roberts.pdf |access-date=21 May 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426045234/http://www2.parl.gc.ca/Sites/LOP/Infoparl/32/1/32n1_09e_Roberts.pdf |archive-date=26 April 2012 }}</ref> [[Canadian sovereignty|Sovereignty]] is conveyed not by the governor general or federal parliament, but through the Crown itself as a part of the executive, legislative and judicial branches of Canada's 11 (one federal and 10 provincial) legal jurisdictions; linking the governments into a federal state,<ref>{{Citation| last=MacLeod| first=Kevin S.| author-link=Kevin S. MacLeod| title=A Crown of Maples| page=17| place=Ottawa| publisher=[[Department of Canadian Heritage]]| year=2012| edition=2012| url=http://canadiancrown.gc.ca/DAMAssetPub/DAM-CRN-jblDmt-dmdJbl/STAGING/texte-text/crnMpls_1336157759317_eng.pdf?WT.contentAuthority=4.4.4| isbn=978-1-100-20079-8| access-date=23 August 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160204231448/http://canadiancrown.gc.ca/DAMAssetPub/DAM-CRN-jblDmt-dmdJbl/STAGING/texte-text/crnMpls_1336157759317_eng.pdf?WT.contentAuthority=4.4.4| archive-date=4 February 2016| url-status=dead}}</ref> the Crown is "divided" into 11 "crowns".<ref>{{cite journal| last=Jackson| first=Michael D.| title=Golden Jubilee and Provincial Crown| journal=Canadian Monarchist News| volume=7| issue=3| page=6| publisher=Monarchist League of Canada| location=Toronto| year=2003| url=http://www.monarchist.ca/sites/default/files/documents/2003/12/186.pdf| access-date=21 May 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150611015926/http://www.monarchist.ca/sites/default/files/documents/2003/12/186.pdf| archive-date=11 June 2015| url-status=dead}}</ref> The fathers of the [[Canadian Confederation]] viewed the constitutional monarchy as a bulwark against potential fracturing of the [[Canadian Confederation|Canadian federation]],<ref>{{cite book| last=Smith| first=David E.| title=The Invisible Crown| url=https://archive.org/details/invisiblecrownfi0000smit| url-access=registration| page=[https://archive.org/details/invisiblecrownfi0000smit/page/8 8]| publisher=University of Toronto Press| year=1995| location=Toronto| isbn=0-8020-7793-5}}</ref> and the Crown remains central to Canadian federalism.<ref>{{Citation| last=Smith| first=David E.| title=The Crown and the Constitution: Sustaining Democracy?| place=Kingston| publisher=Queen's University| date=10 June 2010| page=6| url=http://www.queensu.ca/iigr/conf/Arch/2010/ConferenceOnTheCrown/CrownConferencePapers/The_Crown_and_the_Constitutio1.pdf| access-date=18 May 2010| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017024753/http://www.queensu.ca/iigr/conf/Arch/2010/ConferenceOnTheCrown/CrownConferencePapers/The_Crown_and_the_Constitutio1.pdf| archive-date=17 October 2013}}</ref>
