== Distribution of legislative powers ==
{{See also|Canadian constitutional law}}

[[File:British North America Act, 1867.jpg|thumb|Cover page of the British North America Act, 1867]]

=== Division of powers ===
The '''federal–provincial distribution of legislative powers''' (also known as '''the division of powers''') defines the scope of the federal and provincial legislatures. These have been identified as exclusive to the federal or provincial jurisdictions or shared by all. [[Constitution Act, 1867#Part VI: Division of Powers|Section 91 of the ''Constitution Act, 1867'']], lists the major federal parliament powers, based on the concepts of [[peace, order, and good government]]; while Section 92 of the ''Constitution Act, 1867'' enumerates those of the provincial governments.

The act puts remedial legislation on education rights, uniform laws relating to property and civil rights (in all provinces other than Quebec), creation of a [[Supreme Court of Canada|general court of appeal]] and other courts "for the better Administration of the Laws of Canada," and implementing obligations arising from foreign treaties, all under the purview of the federal legislature in Section 91. Some aspects of the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] were elevated to constitutional status in 1982.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Reference re Supreme Court Act, ss. 5 and 6|link=Reference re Supreme Court Act, ss. 5 and 6|year=2014|court=scc|num=21|date=21 March 2014}}</ref>

The act lists the powers of the provincial parliaments (subject to the federal parliament's authority to regulate inter-provincial movement) in Section 92. These powers include the exploration, development and export to other provinces of non-renewable natural resources, forestry resources and electrical energy. Education is under provincial jurisdiction, subject to the rights of [[separate schools]].

Old-age pensions, agriculture and immigration are shared by federal and provincial jurisdictions. One prevails over the other in cases of conflict, however: for pensions, federal legislation will not displace provincial laws, and for agriculture and immigration it is the reverse.{{why|date=October 2019}}

The ''[[Constitution Act, 1871]]'' allowed parliament to govern any territories not forming part of any province, and the ''[[Statute of Westminster 1931]]'', gave parliament the ability to pass extraterritorial laws.

=== Doctrines ===
To rationalize how each jurisdiction may use its authority, certain doctrines have been devised by the courts: [[pith and substance]]{{Definition needed|date=September 2019}}, including the nature of any ancillary powers and the colourability of legislation{{clarify|date=September 2019}}; [[double aspect]]; [[Paramountcy (Canada)|paramountcy]]; [[inter-jurisdictional immunity]]; the [[living tree doctrine|living tree]]; the [[purposive approach]]; and charter compliance{{Definition needed|date=September 2019}} (most notably through the [[Oakes test]]). Additionally, there is the [[implied Bill of Rights]].

=== Jurisdiction over public property ===

Jurisdiction over Crown property is divided between the provincial legislatures and the federal parliament, with the key provisions Sections 108, 109, and 117 of the ''Constitution Act, 1867''. Public works are the property of the federal Crown, and natural resources are within the purview of the provinces.<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Attorney General for the Dominion of Canada v The Attorneys General for the Provinces of Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia ("Fisheries Case")| court=UKPC| year=1898| num=29| parallelcite=[1898] AC 700| date=26 May 1898| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada}}</ref> Title to such property is not vested in one jurisdiction or another, however, since the Canadian Crown is indivisible.{{sfn|Romney|1999|p=[https://archive.org/details/gettingitwrongho0000romn/page/274 274]}}<ref>{{Citation| last=Cabinet Secretary and Clerk of the Executive Council| title=Executive Government Processes and Procedures in Saskatchewan: A Procedures Manual| place=Regina| publisher=Queen's Printer for Saskatchewan| date=April 2004| page=10| url=http://www.gov.sk.ca/adx/aspx/adxGetMedia.aspx?DocID=635,617,534,206,Documents&MediaID=752&Filename=2004Manual.pdf| access-date=30 July 2009}}</ref> Section 109 has been given a particularly-broad meaning;<ref name="Bowman">{{cite journal| first=Laura| last=Bowman| title=Constitutional "Property" and Reserve Creation: ''Seybold'' Revisited| journal=Manitoba Law Journal| volume=32| issue=1| pages=1–25| publisher=University of Manitoba, Robson Hall Faculty of Law| url=http://dunraven.cc.umanitoba.ca/mlj/images/Articles/32v1/bowman-constitutional%20property.pdf| access-date=17 September 2013| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304042536/http://dunraven.cc.umanitoba.ca/mlj/images/Articles/32v1/bowman-constitutional%20property.pdf| archive-date=4 March 2016| url-status=dead}}</ref> provincial legislation regulating labour used to harvest and the disposal of natural resources does not interfere with federal [[Trade and commerce (Canadian law)|trade and commerce]] power,<ref group="nb">''Smylie v. The Queen'' (1900), 27 O.A.R. 172 (C.A.)</ref>{{sfn|Hogg|2007|loc=par. 29.2}}<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII| litigants=Attorney-General for British Columbia and the Minister of Lands v. Brooks-Bidlake and Whitall, Ltd.| year=1922| court=scc| num=22| format=canlii| parallelcite=63 SCR 466| date=2 July 1922}}</ref>{{sfn|Hogg|2007|loc=par. 29.2}} and royalties have been held to cover the law relating to [[escheat]]s.<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Attorney General of Ontario v Mercer| court=UKPC| year=1883| num=42| parallelcite=[1883] 8 AC 767| date=8 July 1883| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada}}</ref> Canada cannot unilaterally create [[Indian reserve]]s, since the transfer of such lands requires federal and provincial approval by Order in Council (although discussion exists about whether this is sound jurisprudence).<ref name="Bowman" /><ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Ontario Mining Company Limited and The Attorney General for the Dominion of Canada v The Attorney General for the Province of Ontario ("Ontario Mining Co. v. Seybold")| court=UKPC| year=1902| num=46| format=1| parallelcite=[1903] AC 73|date=12 November 1902| juris=Canada}}</ref>

The provincial power to manage [[Crown land]] did not initially extend to [[Manitoba]], [[Alberta]] and [[Saskatchewan]] when they were created from part of the [[Northwest Territories]], since the land was vested in the federal Crown. It was vacated on some land (the [[Railway Belt (British Columbia)|Railway Belt]] and the [[Peace River Block]]) by [[British Columbia]] when it entered the confederation. Title to this land was not vested in those provinces until the passage of the [[Natural Resources Acts]] in 1930. The power is not absolute, however; provincial Crown land may be regulated or expropriated for federal purposes.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII| litigants=Reference re Waters and Water-Powers| year=1929| source=scc| num=72| format=canlii| parallelcite=[1929] SCR 200| date=2 May 1929| courtname=auto}}</ref><ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Attorney General of Quebec v The Nipissing Central Railway Company and another ("Railway Act Reference")| court=UKPC| year=1926| num=39| parallelcite=[1926] AC 715|date=17 May 1926| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada}}</ref> The administration of crown land is also subject to the rights of [[First Nations in Canada|First Nation]]s<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII| litigants=R. v. Sparrow| link=R. v. Sparrow| year=1990| source=scc| num=104| format=canlii| parallelcite=[1990] 1 SCR 1075| date=31 May 1990| courtname=auto}}</ref> (since they are a relevant interest),<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII| litigants=St. Catherines Milling and Lumber Company v The Queen| link=St. Catherines Milling v. The Queen| court=UKPC| year=1888| num=70| format=1| parallelcite=[1888] 14 AC 46| date=12 December 1888| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada}}</ref> and provincial power "is burdened by the Crown obligations toward the Aboriginal people in question".<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII| litigants=Grassy Narrows First Nation v. Ontario (Natural Resources)| year=2014| court=scc| num=48| pinpoint=par. 50| date=11 July 2014}}</ref> Debate exists about whether such burdens apply in the same manner in the Western provinces under the Natural Resources Acts.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://ablawg.ca/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/Blog_KL_Keewatin_July-2014.pdf| first=Kirk| last=Lambrecht| title=The Importance of Location and Context to the Future Application of the ''Grassy Narrows'' Decision of the Supreme Court of Canada| publisher=ABlawg.ca| date=30 July 2014}}</ref>

[[Subsea|Management of offshore resources]] is complex; although management of the beds of [[internal waters]] is vested in the provincial Crowns, management of beds of [[territorial sea]]s is vested in the federal Crown (with management of the [[continental shelf]] and the [[exclusive economic zone]]).<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII| litigants=Reference Re: Offshore Mineral Rights|year=1967| source=scc| num=71| format=canlii| parallelcite=[1967] SCR 792| date=7 November 1967| courtname=auto}}</ref><ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII| litigants=Reference re Newfoundland Continental Shelf|year=1984| source=scc| num=132| format=canlii| pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1984] 1 SCR 86| date=8 March 1984| courtname=auto}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| url=http://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/canadasoceans-oceansducanada/marinezones-zonesmarines-eng.htm| author=Fisheries and Oceans Canada| title=Canada's Ocean Estate – A Description of Canada's Maritime Zones| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=4 September 2012| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080614045543/http://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/oceans/canadasoceans-oceansducanada/marinezones-zonesmarines-eng.htm| archive-date=14 June 2008}}</ref> The beds and islands of the waters between [[Vancouver Island]] and mainland [[British Columbia]] have been declared the property of the [[Monarchy in British Columbia|Crown in right of British Columbia]].<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII| litigants=Reference re: Ownership of the Bed of the Strait of Georgia and Related Areas|year=1984| source=scc| num=138| format=canlii| pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1984] 1 SCR 388| date=17 May 1984| courtname=auto}}</ref> Federal-provincial management agreements have been implemented concerning offshore petroleum resources in the areas around [[Newfoundland and Labrador]] and [[Nova Scotia]].<ref group="na">{{Cite web| url=http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-7.5/index.html|title=Canada-Newfoundland Atlantic Accord Implementation Act (S.C. 1987, c. 3)| access-date=4 September 2012}}</ref><ref group="na">{{Cite web |url=http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-7.8/index.html| title=Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Resources Accord Implementation Act (S.C. 1988, c. 28)| access-date=4 September 2012}}</ref>

=== Taxation and spending ===

[[Taxation in Canada|Taxation]] is a power of the federal and provincial legislatures; provincial taxation is more restricted, in accordance with sections 92(2) and 92(9) of the ''Constitution Act, 1867''. In ''Allard Contractors Ltd. v. Coquitlam (District)'', provincial legislatures may levy an indirect fee as part of a valid regulatory scheme.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII||litigants=Allard Contractors Ltd. v. Coquitlam (District)|year=1993|court=scc|num=45|format=canlii|parallelcite=[1993] 4 SCR 371|date=18 November 1993}}</ref> [[Gérard La Forest]] observed ''[[obiter dictum|obiter dicta]]'' that section 92(9) (with provincial powers over [[property and civil rights]] and matters of a local or private nature) allows for the levying of license fees even if they constitute indirect taxation.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Allocation of Taxing Power Under the Canadian Constitution|url=https://archive.org/details/allocationoftaxi0000lafo|url-access=registration|last=La Forest|first=G.V.|publisher=Canadian Tax Foundation|year=1981|isbn=0-88808006-9|edition=2nd|location=Toronto|page=[https://archive.org/details/allocationoftaxi0000lafo/page/159 159]}}</ref>

Parliament has the power to spend money on public debt and property. Although the Supreme Court of Canada has not ruled directly about constitutional limits on federal spending power,<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Finlay v. Canada (Minister of Finance)|year=1993|court=scc|num=129|format=canlii|pinpoint=par. 29|parallelcite=[1993] 1 SCR 1080|date=25 March 1993}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.parl.gc.ca/Content/LOP/researchpublications/prb0736-e.htm|title=RB 07-36E: The Federal Spending Power|last=Richer|first=Karine|publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada|access-date=16 June 2015}}</ref> parliament can [[Canadian transfer payments|transfer payments]] to the provinces.{{efn|The [[Alberta Court of Appeal]] in ''Winterhaven Stables Limited v. Canada (Attorney General)'' characterized that as possessing the following nature: "[The federal parliament] is entitled to spend the money that it raises through proper exercise of its taxing power in the manner that it chooses to authorize. It can impose conditions on such disposition so long as the conditions do not amount in fact to a regulation or control of a matter outside federal authority. The federal contributions are now made in such a way that they do not control or regulate provincial use of them. As well there are opting out arrangements that are available to those provinces who choose not to participate in certain shared-cost programs.<ref group=nb>{{cite CanLII| litigants=Winterhaven Stables Limited v. Canada (Attorney General)| year=1988| court=abca| num=334| pinpoint=par. 23| parallelcite=53 DLR (4th) 413| date=17 October 1988}}</ref>}} This arises from the 1937 decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on the ''Unemployment Insurance Reference'', where [[Lord Atkin]] observed: "Assuming the Dominion has collected by means of taxation a fund, it by no means follows that any legislation which disposes of it is necessarily within Dominion competence ... If on the true view of the legislation it is found that in reality in pith and substance the legislation invades civil rights within the Province, or in respect of other classes of subjects otherwise encroaches upon the provincial field, the legislation will be invalid".<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=The Attorney General of Canada v The Attorney General of Ontario and others|court=JCPC|year=1937|num=7|format=1|parallelcite=[1937] AC 355|date=28 January 1937|juris=Canada}}</ref> In ''[[Reference re Canada Assistance Plan (B.C.)|Re Canada Assistance Plan]]'', [[John Sopinka|Justice Sopinka]] held that the withholding of federal money previously granted to fund a matter within provincial jurisdiction does not amount to the regulation of that matter.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Reference Re Canada Assistance Plan (B.C.)|link=Reference re Canada Assistance Plan (B.C.)|year=1991|court=scc|num=74|format=canlii|pinpoint=par. 93|parallelcite=[1991] 2 SCR 525|date=15 August 1991}}</ref>

== <span class="anchor" id="Nature of the legislative power within the federal structure"></span>Federal legislative power ==

Much distribution of power has been ambiguous, leading to disputes which have been decided by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and (after 1949) the Supreme Court of Canada. The nature of the Canadian constitution was described by the Privy Council in 1913 as not truly federal (unlike the United States and Australia); although the ''British North America Act, 1867'', states in its preamble that the colonies had expressed "their desire to be federally united into one Dominion", "the natural and literal interpretation of the word [federal] confines its application to cases in which these States, while agreeing on a measure of delegation, yet in the main continue to preserve their original Constitutions". The Privy Council determined that the Fathers of Confederation desired a "general Government charged with matters of common interest, and new and merely local Governments for the Provinces". Matters other than those listed in the ''British North America Act, 1867'', as the responsibility of the federal or provincial parliaments fell to the federal legislature (the reverse of the arrangement between the federal and state congresses in the United States).<ref group=nb>{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Attorney-General for Commonwealth of Australia and others v The Colonial Sugar Refining Company Limited and others| court=UKPC| year=1913| num=76| format=1| parallelcite= [1914] AC 237 |date=17 December 1913|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Australia}}, and stated again in {{cite BAILII| litigants=The Bonanza Creek Gold Mining Company Limited v The King and another|year=1916| court=UKPC| num=11| format=1| parallelcite=[1916] 1 AC 566| date=24 February 1916| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council| juris=Canada}}</ref>

=== National and provincial concerns ===

The preamble of [[Section 91 of the Constitution Act, 1867]] states: "It shall be lawful for the Queen ... to make laws for the Peace, Order, and good Government of Canada, in relation to all Matters not coming within the Classes of Subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the Legislatures of the Provinces". In addition to assigning powers not stated elsewhere (which has been narrowly interpreted), this has led to the creation of the national-emergency and national-concern doctrines.

The national-emergency doctrine was described by [[Jean Beetz|Mr Justice Beetz]] in ''[[Reference re Anti-Inflation Act]]''.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Reference re Anti-Inflation Act|link=Reference re Anti-Inflation Act|year=1976|source=scc|num=16|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1976] 2 SCR 373|date=12 July 1976|courtname=auto|juris=}}, 463{{endash}}464</ref>{{efn|
"But if one looks at the practical effects of the exercise of the emergency power, one must conclude that it operates so as to give to Parliament for all purposes necessary to deal with the emergency, concurrent and paramount jurisdiction over matters which would normally fall within exclusive provincial jurisdiction. To that extent, the exercise of that power amounts to a temporary ''[[pro tanto]]'' amendment of a federal Constitution by the unilateral action of Parliament. The legitimacy of that power is derived from the Constitution: when the security and the continuation of the Constitution and of the nation are at stake, the kind of power commensurate with the situation 'is only to be found in that part of the Constitution which establishes power in the State as a whole'."<ref group="nb">[[Viscount Haldane]] in ''[[Fort Frances Pulp and Paper v. Manitoba Free Press|Fort Frances]]'', p. 704</ref>}}{{efn|"The extraordinary nature and the constitutional features of the emergency power of Parliament dictate the manner and form in which it should be invoked and exercised. It should not be an ordinary manner and form. At the very least, it cannot be a manner and form which admits of the slightest degree of ambiguity to be resolved by interpretation. In cases where the existence of an emergency may be a matter of controversy, it is imperative that Parliament should not have recourse to its emergency power except in the most explicit terms indicating that it is acting on the basis of that power. Parliament cannot enter the normally forbidden area of provincial jurisdiction unless it gives an unmistakable signal that it is acting pursuant to its extraordinary power. Such a signal is not conclusive to support the legitimacy of the action of Parliament but its absence is fatal."}} The national-concern doctrine is governed by the principles stated by [[Gerald Le Dain|Mr Justice Le Dain]] in ''[[R. v. Crown Zellerbach Canada Ltd.]]''.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=R. v. Crown Zellerbach Canada Ltd.|link=R. v. Crown Zellerbach Canada Ltd.|year=1988|source=scc|num=63|format=canlii|pinpoint=par. 33|parallelcite=49 DLR (4th) 161; [1988] 3 WWR 385|date=24 March 1988|courtname=auto|juris=}}</ref>{{efn|

# The national concern doctrine is separate and distinct from the national emergency doctrine of the peace, order and good government power, which is chiefly distinguishable by the fact that it provides a constitutional basis for what is necessarily legislation of a temporary nature;
# The national concern doctrine applies to both new matters which did not exist at Confederation and to matters which, although originally matters of a local or private nature in a province, have since, in the absence of national emergency, become matters of national concern;
# For a matter to qualify as a matter of national concern in either sense it must have a singleness, distinctiveness and indivisibility that clearly distinguishes it from matters of provincial concern and a scale of impact on provincial jurisdiction that is reconcilable with the fundamental distribution of legislative power under the Constitution;
# In determining whether a matter has attained the required degree of singleness, distinctiveness and indivisibility that clearly distinguishes it from matters of provincial concern it is relevant to consider what would be the effect on extra‑provincial interests of a provincial failure to deal effectively with the control or regulation of the intra‑provincial aspects of the matter.}}

The federal government is partially limited by powers assigned to the provincial legislatures; for example, the Canadian constitution created broad provincial jurisdiction over direct taxation and [[property and civil rights]]. Many disputes between the two levels of government revolve around conflicting interpretations of the meaning of these powers.

In the ''[[Local Prohibition Case]]'' of 1896, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council arrived at a method of interpretation, known as the "four-departments doctrine", in which jurisdiction over a matter is determined in the following order:<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=The Attorney General for Ontario v The Attorney General for the Dominion of Canada, and the Distillers and Brewers' Association of Ontario|link=|court=UKPC|year=1896|num=20|parallelcite = [1896] AC 348|date=9 May 1896|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Canada|format=1}}</ref>

# Does it fall under Section 92, classes 1{{endash}}15?
# Can it be characterized as falling under Section 91, classes 1{{endash}}29?
# Is it of a general nature, bringing it within Section 91's residuary clause?
# If not, it falls under Section 92, class 16.<ref>for example, {{Cite web|author = Claude Bélanger|title = Theories and Interpretation of the ''Constitution Act, 1867''|url = http://faculty.marianopolis.edu/c.belanger/quebechistory/federal/interpret.htm|publisher = [[Marianopolis College]]|access-date = 9 October 2012}}</ref>

[[File:1stViscountSankey.jpg|thumb|right|alt=Formal photo of a judge in wig and robe|[[John Sankey, 1st Viscount Sankey|Lord Sankey]]]]

By the 1930s, as noted in the ''[[Fish Canneries Reference]]'' and ''[[In re Regulation and Control of Aeronautics in Canada|Aeronautics Reference]]'', the division of responsibilities between federal and provincial jurisdictions was summarized by [[John Sankey, 1st Viscount Sankey|Lord Sankey]].{{efn|''[[In re Regulation and Control of Aeronautics in Canada|Aeronautics Reference]]'' at p. 8: # The legislation of the Parliament of the Dominion, so long as it strictly relates to subjects of legislation expressly enumerated in section 91, is of paramount authority, even if it trenches upon matters assigned to the Provincial Legislature by section 92.

# The general power of legislation conferred up on the Parliament of the Dominion by section 91 of the act in supplement of the power to legislate upon the subjects expressly enumerated must be strictly confined to such matters as are unquestionably of national interest and importance, and must not trench on any of the subjects enumerated in section 92, as within the scope of Provincial legislation, unless these matters have attained such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the Dominion.
# It is within the competence of the Dominion Parliament to provide for matters which though otherwise within the legislative competence of the Provincial Legislature, are necessarily incidental to effective legislation by the Parliament of the Dominion upon a subject of legislation expressly enumerated in section 91.
# There can be a domain in which Provincial and Dominion legislation may overlap, in which case, neither legislation will be ''ultra vires'' if the field is clear, but if the field is not clear and the two legislations meet, the Dominion legislation must prevail.}}

Although the Statute of Westminster 1931 declared that the Parliament of Canada had [[extraterritorial jurisdiction]], the provincial legislatures did not achieve similar status. According to [[Section 92 of the Constitution Act, 1867|s. 92]], "In each Province the Legislature may exclusively make Laws ...".

If a provincial law affects the rights of individuals outside the province:

:* If it is, in [[pith and substance]], provincial, ancillary effects on the rights of individuals outside the province are irrelevant<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=Edgar F. Ladore and others v George Bennett and others|link=|court=UKPC|year=1939|num=33|parallelcite=[1939] 3 D.L.R. 1, [1939] AC. 468|date=8 May 1939|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Ontario|format = 1}}</ref> but
:* Where it is, in pith and substance, legislation in relation to the rights of individuals outside the province, it will be ''[[ultra vires]]'' the province<ref name="RBC-King" group="nb">{{cite BAILII| litigants=The Royal Bank of Canada and others v The King and another| court=UKPC| year=1913| num=1a| parallelcite=[1913] A.C. 212| date=31 January 1913| courtname=Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|juris=Alberta |format=1}}</ref><ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Re Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act|link=Re Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act|year=1984|source=scc|num=17|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1984] 1 SCR 297|date=3 May 1984|courtname=auto|juris=}}</ref>

In ''The Queen (Man.) v. Air Canada'', it was held that the s. 92(2) power providing for "direct taxation within the province" does not extend to taxing sales on flights passing over (or through) a province, but the question of how far provincial jurisdiction can extend into a province's [[airspace]] was left undecided.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=The Queen (Man.) v. Air Canada|link=|year=1980|source=scc|num=16|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1980] 2 SCR 303|date=18 July 1980|courtname=auto|juris=}}</ref> However, the [[property and civil rights]] power does allow for determining rules with respect to [[conflict of laws]] in civil matters.<ref group="na">for example, {{Cite web|title = ''Court Jurisdiction and Proceedings Transfer Act'', SBC 2003, c. 28|url = http://www.bclaws.ca/EPLibraries/bclaws_new/document/ID/freeside/00_03028_01|publisher = Queen's Printer of British Columbia|access-date = 5 September 2012}}</ref>

=== <span class="anchor" id="Attaining a national dimension"></span>National dimension ===

Federal jurisdiction arises in several circumstances:

:* Under the national-emergency doctrine for temporary legislation (the ''[[War Measures Act]]'')
:* Under the national-concern doctrine for:
:** Matters not existing at confederation (radio and television)
:** Matters of a local or private nature in a province which have become matters of national concern, such as what can accrue to [[Section 91(2) of the Constitution Act, 1867|the regulation of trade and commerce]]
:* Matters where the grant is exclusive under [[Section 91 of the Constitution Act, 1867|Section 91]] ([[Section 91(27) of the Constitution Act, 1867|criminal law]])
:* Matters where authority may be assumed (as with [[Section 92(10) of the Constitution Act, 1867|works for the general advantage of Canada]])

The [[Peace, order, and good government#The Gap Branch|gap approach]], employed sparingly, identifies areas of jurisdiction arising from oversights by the drafters of the constitution; for example, federal jurisdiction to incorporate companies is inferred from the power provinces have under Section 92 for "The Incorporation of Companies with Provincial Objects".

=== Uniformity of federal law ===

Section 129 of the ''Constitution Act, 1867'' provided for laws in effect at the time of Confederation to continue until repealed or altered by the appropriate legislative authority. Similar provisions were included in the terms of union of other territories that were subsequently incorporated into Canada.

The uniformity of laws in some areas of federal jurisdiction was significantly delayed. Offences were not made uniform until 1892, when common-law criminal offences were abolished under the ''[[Criminal Code (Canada)|Criminal Code, 1892]]''.<ref>''Criminal Code, 1892'', SC 1892, c 29</ref> [[Divorce Act (Canada)|Divorce law]] was not made uniform until 1968, [[Canadian maritime law]] not until 1971 and [[Civil Marriage Act|marriage law]] not until 2005. Provisions of the ''[[Civil Code of Lower Canada]]'', adopted in 1865 by the former Province of Canada, affecting federal jurisdiction continued to be in force in Quebec (if they had not been displaced by other federal Acts) until their repeal on 15 December 2004.<ref group="na">{{Cite web|title = ''Federal Law-Civil Law Harmonization Act, No. 1'', S.C. 2001, c. 4, s. 3|url = http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/AnnualStatutes/2001_4/page-1.html#h-4|access-date = 8 August 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Backgrounder: A Third Bill to Harmonize Federal Law with the Civil Law of Quebec|url = http://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/news-nouv/nr-cp/2010/doc_32559.html|publisher = [[Department of Justice (Canada)]]|access-date = 8 August 2012|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120323222606/http://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/news-nouv/nr-cp/2010/doc_32559.html|archive-date = 23 March 2012|url-status = dead}}</ref>

=== Interplay of jurisdictions ===

[[File:Supreme Court of Canada, Ottawa.jpg|thumb|right|alt=Large grey building in winter, with a Canadian flag in front|[[Supreme Court of Canada]]]]

According to the Supreme Court of Canada, "our Constitution is based on an allocation of exclusive powers to both levels of government, not concurrent powers, although these powers are bound to interact in the realities of the life of our Constitution."<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Canadian Western Bank v. Alberta|link=Canadian Western Bank v. Alberta|year=2007|source=scc|num=22|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[2007] 2 SCR 3|date=31 May 2007|courtname=|juris=|ref={{harvid|Canadian Western Bank|2007}}}}, par. 32</ref> [[Brian Dickson|Chief Justice Dickson]] observed the complexity of that interaction:

<blockquote>The history of Canadian constitutional law has been to allow for a fair amount of interplay and indeed overlap between federal and provincial powers. It is true that doctrines like interjurisdictional and Crown immunity and concepts like "watertight compartments" qualify the extent of that interplay. But it must be recognized that these doctrines and concepts have not been the dominant tide of constitutional doctrines; rather they have been an undertow against the strong pull of pith and substance, the aspect doctrine and, in recent years, a very restrained approach to concurrency and paramountcy issues.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Ontario (Attorney General) v. OPSEU|link=|year=1987|source=scc|num=71|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1987] 2 SCR 2|date=29 July 1987|courtname=|juris=}} at par. 27</ref>
</blockquote>

Notable examples include:
* Although the provinces have the power to create [[Criminal law|criminal courts]], only the federal government has the power to determine [[Section 91(27) of the Constitution Act, 1867|criminal procedure]]. Criminal procedure includes [[prosecution]], and federal law can determine the extent of federal and provincial involvement.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Attorney General of Canada v. Canadian National Transportation, Ltd.|link=|year=1983|source=scc|num=36|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1983] 2 SCR 206|courtname=auto|juris=}}</ref> The provinces' power under [[Section 92(14) of the Constitution Act, 1867|s. 92(14)]] over the [[administration of justice]] includes the organization of [[court]]s and [[police force]]s, which determines the level of [[Law enforcement in Canada|law enforcement]]. The [[Royal Canadian Mounted Police]], as the federal police, contracts for the provision of many provincial and municipal police forces.
* Although the federal power to regulate fisheries does not override provincial authority to require a permit for catching fish in waters under provincial control,<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=The Attorney General for the Dominion of Canada v The Attorneys General for the Provinces of Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia ("Fisheries Reference")|link=|court=UKPC|year=1898|num=29|parallelcite=[1898] A.C. 700|date=26 May 1898|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Canada|format = 1}}</ref> the regulation of [[recreational fishing|recreational fisheries]] has been partially delegated under the ''Fisheries Act''<ref group="na">{{Cite web|url = http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/F-14/index.html|title = ''Fisheries Act'' (R.S.C., 1985, c. F-14)|access-date = 4 September 2012}}</ref> to the provinces for specified species in specific provinces.<ref group="na">{{Cite web|title = Recreational Fishing Regulations|date = 16 November 2007|url = http://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/fm-gp/peches-fisheries/rec/regs-eng.htm|publisher = [[Fisheries and Oceans Canada]]|access-date = 4 September 2012}}</ref>
* Works affecting [[navigation]] are subject to federal approval under the ''[[Navigable Waters Protection Act]]''<ref>{{Cite web|title = NWPA Regulatory Framework |url = http://www.tc.gc.ca/eng/marinesafety/oep-nwpp-framework-250.htm|publisher = Transport Canada|access-date = 22 August 2012}}</ref> and provincial approval, since the beds of navigable waters are generally reserved to the Crown in right of the province.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Policy PL 2.02.02 – Ownership determinations – Beds of navigable waters|url = http://www.mnr.gov.on.ca/stdprodconsume/groups/lr/@mnr/@crownland/documents/document/mnr_e000115.pdf|publisher = Ministry of Natural Resources of Ontario|date = 26 February 2007|access-date = 22 August 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Procedure PL 2.02.02 – Ownership determinations – Beds of navigable waters|url = http://www.mnr.gov.on.ca/stdprodconsume/groups/lr/@mnr/@crownland/documents/document/243950.pdf|publisher = Ministry of Natural Resources of Ontario|date = 26 February 2007|access-date = 22 August 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Dams, Water Crossings and Channelizations – The Lakes and Rivers Improvement Act|url = http://www.mnr.gov.on.ca/en/Business/Water/2ColumnSubPage/STDPROD_088392.html|publisher = Ministry of Natural Resources of Ontario|access-date = 22 August 2012}}</ref>
* Although federal jurisdiction over [[broadcasting]] and most [[telecommunications]] is exclusive, the provinces may regulate advertising<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Attorney General of Quebec v. Kellogg's Co. of Canada|link=Attorney General of Quebec v. Kellogg's Co. of Canada|year=1978|source=scc|num=185|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1978] 2 SCR 211|date=19 January 1978|courtname=auto|juris=}}</ref> and cable installation (above or underground).<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=The Corporation of the City of Toronto v The Bell Telephone Company of Canada|link=|court=UKPC|division=|year=1904|num=71|parallelcite=|date=11 November 1904|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Ontario|format = 1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Canadian Municipalities and the Regulation of Radio Antennae and their Support Structures {{emdash}} III. An Analysis of Constitutional Jurisdiction in Relation to Radiocommunication |date = 6 December 2004|url = http://www.ic.gc.ca/eic/site/smt-gst.nsf/eng/sf09387.html|publisher = [[Industry Canada]]|access-date = 9 October 2012}}</ref>
* Although the concept of [[marriage]] is under federal jurisdiction, the [[Wedding|solemnization of marriage]]s is controlled by the provinces.
* The provincial power to regulate [[security interest]]s under the [[Section 92(13) of the Constitution Act, 1867|property and civil-rights power]] will be displaced by security interests created under a federal head of power – most notably under the [[Bank Act (Canada)|banking power]] – but only to the extent that federal law has covered the field.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Bank of Montreal v. Innovation Credit Union|link=Bank of Montreal v. Innovation Credit Union|year=2010|source=scc|num=47|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[2010] 3 SCR 3|date=5 November 2010|courtname=|juris=}}</ref>
* Laws arising from the property and civil-rights power will be used to complement the interpretation of federal legislation where the federal Act has not provided otherwise, but federal power cannot be used to create rules of private law in areas outside its jurisdiction.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Clark v. Canadian National Railway Co.|link=|year=1988|source=scc|num=18|format=canlii|parallelcite=[1988] 2 SCR 680|date=15 December 1988|courtname=|juris=}}</ref><ref group="na">{{cite web|title = ''Interpretation Act'' (R.S.C., 1985, c. I-21)|date = 26 February 2015|url = http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/I-21/section-8.1.html}} codifies the general rule at s. 8.1.</ref>
* In [[Insolvency law of Canada|insolvency law]], provincial statutes operate by federal incorporation into the ''[[Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act]]'' and the ''[[Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act]]''. However, where a stay under federal law has been lifted in order to allow proceedings to take place, a province can impose a [[Moratorium (law)|moratorium]] on proceedings falling under provincial law.<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=Abitibi Power and Paper Company Limited v Montreal Trust Company and others|link=|court=UKPC|year=1943|num=37|format=1|parallelcite= [1943] AC 536 |date=8 July 1943|juris=Ontario}}, upholding {{Cite canlaw|short title = The Abitibi Power and Paper Company Limited Moratorium Act, 1941|abbr = S.O.|year = 1941|chapter = 1|link = https://archive.org/stream/statutesofprovin1941onta#page/n13/mode/2up}}</ref>

=== Delegation and cooperation ===

In 1899, [[William Watson, Baron Watson|Lord Watson]] asserted during the argument in ''CPR v Bonsecours''<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=Canadian Pacific Railway Company v The Corporation of the Parish of Notre Dame De Bonsecour|link=|court=UKPC|year=1899|num=22|parallelcite=[1899] AC 367|date=24 March 1899|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Quebec}}</ref> that neither the federal parliament nor the provincial legislatures could give legislative authority to the other level.{{sfn|La Forest|1975|p=134}} Subsequent attempts to dovetail federal and provincial legislation to achieve certain ends met with difficulty, such as an attempt by Saskatchewan to ensure enforcement of a federal statute<ref group="na">''Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act'', R.S.C. 1927, c.120</ref> by enacting a complementary Act<ref group="na">{{Cite canlaw|short title  =Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act|abbr =R.S.S.|year =1930|chapter =151|link =http://www.qp.gov.sk.ca/documents/english/statutes/historical/1930-CH-151.pdf}}</ref> declaring that the federal Act would continue in force under provincial authority if it was ruled ''[[ultra vires]]''. The [[Saskatchewan Court of Appeal]] ruled a federal and provincial Act ''ultra vires'', voiding both as an attempt by the province to vest powers in parliament unauthorized by the ''BNA Act''.{{sfn|La Forest|1975|p=135}}<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=R. v. Zaslavsky|link=|year=1935|court=skca|num=142|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1935] 3 DLR 788|date=15 April 1935|courtname=auto|juris=}}</ref>

The matter was addressed in 1950 by the Supreme Court,{{sfn|La Forest|1975|pp=135{{endash}}137}} which held ''ultra vires'' a proposed Nova Scotia Act which would have authorized the inter-delegation of legislative and taxation authority between Parliament and the Nova Scotia legislature.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. Attorney General of Canada (the "Nova Scotia Inter-delegation case")|link=|year=1950|court=scc|num=26|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1951] SCR 31|date=3 October 1950 }}</ref> In that decision, [[Ivan Rand|Justice Rand]] explained the distinction between delegation to a subordinate body and that to a legislative body.{{efn|
"In the generality of actual delegation to its own agencies, Parliament, recognizing the need of the legislation, lays down the broad scheme and indicates the principles, purposes and scope of the subsidiary details to be supplied by the delegate: under the mode of enactment now being considered, the real and substantial analysis and weighing of the political considerations which would decide the actual provisions adopted, would be given by persons chosen to represent local interests.

Since neither is a creature nor a subordinate body of the other, the question is not only or chiefly whether one can delegate, but whether the other can accept. Delegation implies subordination and in ''[[Hodge v. The Queen]]'', the following observations ... appear:

Within these limits of subjects and area the local legislature is supreme, and has the same authority as the Imperial Parliament, or the parliament of the Dominion, would have had under like circumstances to confide to a municipal institution or body of its own creation authority to make by-laws or resolutions as to subjects specified in the enactment, and with the object of carrying the enactment into operation and effect....

It was argued at the bar that a legislature committing important regulations to agents or delegates effaces itself. That is not so. It retains its powers intact, and can, whenever it pleases, destroy the agency it has created and set up another, or take the matter directly into his own hands. How far it shall seek the aid of subordinate agencies, and how long it shall continue them, are matters for each legislature, and not for Courts of Law, to decide."
}}

Later attempts to achieve federal-provincial coordination have succeeded with other types of legislative schemes{{sfn|La Forest|1975|p=137{{endash}}143}} involving:
* Conditional legislation (such as a federal Act, providing that it will not apply where a provincial Act has been enacted in a given matter). As Justice Rand declared in 1959, "That Parliament can so limit the operation of its own legislation and that it may do so upon any such event or condition is not open to serious debate".<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=Lord's Day Alliance v. Attorney-General of British Columbia|link=|year=1959|court=scc|num=42|format=canlii|pinpoint=|parallelcite=[1959] SCR 497|date=28 April 1959 }}</ref>
* Incorporation by reference or adoption (for example, a federal regulation prohibiting vehicles from operating on a federal highway except "in accordance with the laws of the province and the municipality in which the highway is situated")<ref group="na">{{Cite canlaw|short title  =Government Property Traffic Regulations|abbr =C.R.C.|year =1977|chapter = 887|section =6|subsection =1|link =http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/C.R.C.,_c._887/section-6.html}}</ref>
* Joint schemes with administrative cooperation, such as the administrative authority granted by federal law to provincial transport boards to license extraprovincial transport<ref group="na">{{Cite canlaw|short title  =Motor Vehicle Transport Act |abbr =R.S.C.|year =1985|chapter =29 (3rd Supp.)|section =7|link =http://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/M-12.01/section-7.html}}</ref>

=== <span class="anchor" id="The power to implement treaties"></span>Power to implement treaties ===

To understand how treaties can enter Canadian law, three significant cases must be considered: the ''[[In re Regulation and Control of Aeronautics in Canada|Aeronautics Reference]]'', the ''[[Radio Reference]]'' and the ''[[Labour Conventions Reference]]''.<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=The Attorney General of Canada v The Attorney General of Ontario and others ("Labour Conventions Reference")|link=Labour Conventions Reference|court=UKPC|year=1937|num=6|parallelcite=[1937] A.C. 326|date=28 January 1937|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Canada|format = 1}}</ref> Although the reasoning behind the judgments is complex,<ref>{{cite book |title= Canadian Federalism and Treaty Powers: Organic Constitutionalism at Work|last= Cyr|first= Hugo|year= 2009|publisher= P.I.E. Peter Lang SA|location= Brussels|isbn= 978-90-5201-453-1|chapter= I {{endash}} The ''Labour Conventions'' Case|access-date=29 August 2012 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g9-6tXGTru8C&q=radio+reference+and+canadian+federalism&pg=PA61}}</ref> it is considered to break down as follows:
* [[Aeronautics]] were held by the ''Aeronautics Reference'' to be within the authority of the Parliament of Canada under s. 132 governing treaties entered into by the British Empire. After that treaty was replaced, it was held in ''[[Johannesson v. West St. Paul]]'' that in accordance with ''[[Ontario v. Canada Temperance Federation]]'' the field continued to be within federal jurisdiction under the power relating to [[peace, order and good government]].
* Although an international agreement governing [[broadcasting]] was not a treaty of the British Empire, the ''Radio Reference'' held that it fell within federal jurisdiction; Canada's obligations under its agreements in this field required it to pass legislation applying to all Canadian residents, and the matter could be seen as analogous to [[telegraph]]s (already in the federal sphere).
* The ''Labour Conventions Reference'' dealt with labour relations (clearly within provincial jurisdiction); since the conventions were not treaties of the British Empire and no plausible argument could be made for the field attaining a national dimension or becoming of national concern, the Canadian Parliament was unable to exercise new legislative authority.

Although the ''[[Statute of Westminster 1931]]'' had made Canada fully independent in governing its foreign affairs, the [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council]] held that s. 132 did not evolve to take that into account. As noted by [[Lord Atkin]] at the end of the judgment,

<blockquote>It must not be thought that the result of this decision is that Canada is incompetent to legislate in performance of treaty obligations. In totality of legislative powers, Dominion and Provincial together, she is fully equipped. But the legislative powers remain distributed and if in the exercise of her new functions derived from her new international status she incurs obligations they must, so far as legislation be concerned when they deal with provincial classes of subjects, be dealt with by the totality of powers, in other words by co-operation between the Dominion and the Provinces. While the ship of state now sails on larger ventures and into foreign waters she still retains the watertight compartments which are an essential part of her original structure.
</blockquote>

This case left undecided the extent of federal power to negotiate, sign and ratify treaties dealing with areas under provincial jurisdiction, and has generated extensive debate about complications introduced in implementing Canada's subsequent international obligations;<ref>{{Cite web|author = Zagros Madjd-Sadjadi, Winston-Salem State University|title = ''Subnational Sabotage or National Paramountcy? Examining the Dynamics of Subnational Acceptance of International Agreements''|url = http://www.sacscanada.org/SJCSv2n1/Sadjadi.pdf|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130711083736/http://www.sacscanada.org/SJCSv2n1/Sadjadi.pdf|url-status = usurped|archive-date = 11 July 2013|publisher = Southern Journal of Canadian Studies, vol. 2, 1|access-date = 12 January 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|editor1 = Yves Le Bouthillier|editor2 = Donald M. McRae|editor3 = Donat Pharand|author = H. Scott Fairley|title = Selected Papers in International Law: Contribution of the Canadian Council on International Law|chapter = External Affairs and the Canadian Constitution|publisher = Kluwer International|location = London|isbn = 90-411-9764-8|pages = 79{{endash}}91|year = 1999}}</ref> the Supreme Court of Canada has indicated in several ''[[obiter dictum|dicta]]'' that it might revisit the issue in an appropriate case.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mcgill.ca/maritimelaw/maritime-admiralty/interpretation/#N_25_|title=Canadian Interpretation and Construction of Maritime Conventions|access-date=23 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140909053445/http://www.mcgill.ca/maritimelaw/maritime-admiralty/interpretation#N_25_|archive-date=9 September 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Limits on legislative power ==

Outside the questions of ''[[ultra vires]]'' and compliance with the ''[[Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms]]'', there are absolute limits on what the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures can legislate. According to the ''Constitution Act, 1867'':
* S. 96 has been construed to hold that neither the provincial legislatures nor Parliament can enact legislation removing part of the inherent jurisdiction of the superior courts.<ref group="nb">{{cite CanLII|litigants=MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v. Simpson|link=MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v. Simpson|year=1995|court=scc|num=57|format=canlii|parallelcite=[1995] 4 SCR 725|date=14 December 1995}}; {{cite CanLII|litigants=Re Residential Tenancies Act|link=Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979|year=1981|court=scc|num=24|format=24|parallelcite=[1981] 1 SCR 714|date=28 May 1981}}; {{cite CanLII|litigants=Crevier v. A.G. (Québec) et al.|link=Crevier v. Quebec|year=1981|court=scc|num=30|format=canlii|parallelcite=[1981] 2 SCR 220|date=20 October 1981}}; {{cite CanLII|litigants=Trial Lawyers Association of British Columbia v. British Columbia (Attorney General)|link=Trial Lawyers Association of British Columbia v. British Columbia (Attorney General)|year=2014|court=scc|num=59|parallelcite=|date=2 October 2014}}</ref>
* [[Section 121 of the Constitution Act, 1867|S. 121]] states, "All Articles of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture of any one of the Provinces shall, from and after the Union, be admitted free into each of the other Provinces". This amounts to a prohibition of inter-provincial [[tariff]]s.
* [[Section 125 of the Constitution Act, 1867|S. 125]] states, "No Lands or Property belonging to Canada or any Province shall be liable to Taxation".
* Under s. 129, limits have been placed on the ability of the legislatures of Ontario and Quebec to amend or repeal Acts of the former [[Province of Canada]]. Where such an act created a [[body corporate]] operating in the former Province, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council held that such bodies cannot have "provincial objects" and only the Parliament of Canada had power to deal with such acts.<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=Rev. Robert Dobie v The Board for Management of the Presbyterian Church of Canada|link=|court=UKPC|year=1882|num=4|parallelcite=7 App Cas 136 |date=21 January 1882|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Quebec|format=1}}</ref> It has been held that this restriction exists for any Act applying equally to Upper and Lower Canada,{{efn|''Ex parte O'Neill'', RJQ 24 SC 304,<ref>{{cite book |last= Lefroy|first= Augustus Henry Frazer|year= 1918|title= A short treatise on Canadian constitutional law|url= https://archive.org/stream/shorttreatiseonc00lefrrich#page/188/mode/2up|location= Toronto|publisher= The Carswell Company|page= 189}}</ref> where it was held that the Legislative Assembly of Quebec was unable to repeal the ''Temperance Act, 1864'',<ref group="na">{{Cite canlaw|short title  =An Act to amend the laws in force respecting the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors and the issue of Licenses therefor, and otherwise for repression of abuses resulting from such sale|abbr =S.C.|year =1864|chapter = 18|link= https://books.google.com/books?id=AHCuAAAAMAAJ&lpg=PA165&ots=SI-wiQmTCo&pg=PA146#v=onepage&f=false}}</ref> but it could pass a concurrent statute for regulating liquor traffic within the Province.<ref>{{cite book |last= Lefroy|first= Augustus Henry Frazer|year= 1913|title= Canada's Federal System|url= https://archive.org/stream/canadasfederalsy00lefr#page/162/mode/2up|location= Toronto|publisher= The Carswell Company|pages= 162{{endash}}163}}</ref> However, it has also been held that the Parliament of Canada could not repeal that Act with respect only to Ontario.<ref group="nb">{{cite BAILII|litigants=The Attorney General for Ontario v The Attorney General for the Dominion of Canada, and the Distillers and Brewers' Association of Ontario (The "Local Prohibition Case")|link=Local Prohibition Case|court=UKPC|year=1896|num=20|parallelcite = [1896] AC 348|date=9 May 1896|courtname=[[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council|P.C.]]|juris=Canada|format=1}}</ref>}} which became problematic when the ''[[Civil Code of Lower Canada]]'' was replaced by the ''[[Civil Code of Quebec]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last= Leclair|first= Jean|year= 1999|title= The Harmonization of Federal Legislation with the Civil Law of the Province of Quebec and Canadian Bijuralism|chapter = Thoughts on the Constitutional Problems Raised by the Repeal of the ''Civil Code of Lower Canada''|url= https://papyrus.bib.umontreal.ca/xmlui/bitstream/handle/1866/3648/Thoughts%20on%20The%20Constitutional%20Problems.pdf;jsessionid=B7F7D13FA08D83CCFD07D7AF286740FB?sequence=1|location= Ottawa|publisher= Department of Justice|pages= 347{{endash}}394}}</ref>

While the Parliament of Canada has the ability to bind the Crown in right of Canada or of any province, the converse is not true for the provincial legislatures, as "[p]rovincial legislation cannot ''proprio vigore'' [ie, of its own force] take away or abridge any privilege of the Crown in right of the Dominion."<ref group="nb">per [[Charles Fitzpatrick|Fitzpatrick CJ]], in {{cite CanLII|litigants=Gauthier v The King|link=|year=1918|court=scc|num=85|format=canlii|pinpoint=p. 194|parallelcite=[1918] 56 SCR 176|date=1918-03-05|courtname=auto|juris=}}</ref>
